question: Which properties of an input data set can and cannot be inferred from a stationary t-SNE visualization, specifically for cluster salience, perturbation stability, poison points, and extreme outliers?

key_findings.claim: A single stationary t-SNE visualization does not identify the strength of the input clustering.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 constructs, for any eligible partition and every scale 0 < epsilon <= 1, an input whose mean silhouette score is multiplied by epsilon while the entire set of stationary t-SNE outputs is unchanged for every perplexity. Corollary 4 specializes this to a perfectly clustered output shared by inputs spanning silhouette scores from arbitrarily close to zero through one.

anchors.section: 4.1 Different Inputs, Same Output, Theorem 3 and Corollary 4

key_findings.claim: Near-equidistant inputs can support arbitrarily different stationary t-SNE outputs.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5 states that any two attainable stationary outputs can be induced by two inputs whose corresponding squared pairwise distances differ by at most a multiplicative 1 +/- epsilon. The construction exploits additive invariance of the input affinities; experiments perturb a regular simplex by only epsilon = 0.01 and obtain qualitatively distinct plots.

anchors.section: 4.2.1 Instability under Small Distance Perturbations, Theorem 5

key_findings.claim: One strategically placed point can erase cluster evidence in the t-SNE loss landscape.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 7 constructs an unclustered data set and a data set with silhouette score at least (sqrt(3)-1)/sqrt(3), approximately 0.42, that have identical stationary t-SNE sets after the same point is inserted at perplexity one. Synthetic Gaussian and BBC/RoBERTa experiments show related degradation at practical perplexities because the inserted central point becomes a nearest neighbor to much of a near-simplex cloud.

anchors.section: 4.2.2 Instability under Insertion of a Single Point, Theorem 7

key_findings.claim: No stationary t-SNE output can faithfully display arbitrarily extreme outlier separation under the paper's geometric outlier number.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 9 bounds the output outlier number by 3.266 + o_n(1), independently of the input. The proof uses the nonzero gradient that an excessively isolated output point would induce and the asymmetry between normalized input and output affinities.

anchors.section: 5 Misrepresentation of Outliers, Definition 8 and Theorem 9

key_findings.claim: The empirical examples demonstrate the predicted mechanisms but do not estimate how frequently the adversarial regimes arise without deliberate construction.
key_findings.evidence: The experiments cover a PBMC3k impostor, near-simplex perturbations, Gaussian mixtures, credit-card fraud, and BBC text embeddings. They instantiate the proofs and show practical failures, but there is no sampling frame over ordinary analysis workflows, blinded user interpretation, uncertainty interval, or benchmark-wide failure-rate estimate.

method.core_idea: Analyze the map from Euclidean input distances to t-SNE affinities and stationary loss points, then construct pairs of metrically different inputs that the affinity normalization makes indistinguishable.
method.mechanism: Adding a common constant to all squared pairwise distances can preserve the perplexity-calibrated conditional affinities after rescaling bandwidths. Schoenberg-style Euclidean distance constructions turn that algebraic invariance into realizable data sets. Separate gradient bounds show that the normalized output affinity cannot support a sufficiently isolated stationary point.
assumptions: The formal target is the set of stationary points of the standard symmetric t-SNE objective, not the stochastic distribution of outputs produced by a particular implementation and seed.
The main constructions allow input dimension n-1 and therefore establish non-identifiability in high dimension rather than a calibrated failure probability for a fixed application dimension.
The poison-point identity theorem uses perplexity one, while practical-perplexity behavior is supported empirically rather than by the same exact theorem.
Cluster strength is formalized primarily with silhouette score; appendices extend the construction to Calinski-Harabasz and Dunn indices.

techniques.role: Preserves t-SNE input affinities while continuously changing the geometry and cluster index of the input.
Strengthens an optimizer-specific counterexample by showing equality of all stationary outputs for paired inputs.
Upper-bounds how isolated a point may be in any stationary t-SNE embedding.
Turns the theoretical affinity failure into impostor, small-perturbation, poison-point, and outlier experiments.

evaluations.setting: PBMC3k single-cell data with 2,638 points represented in 50 dimensions
evaluations.metric: Input silhouette and visual/interpoint-distance comparison under the same two-dimensional t-SNE output
evaluations.result: A constructed impostor with much weaker cluster separation produces essentially the same t-SNE visualization as the real data while preserving neighbor order.

evaluations.setting: Regular-simplex and high-dimensional Gaussian-mixture synthetic data
evaluations.metric: Qualitative embedding change, silhouette score, and response to one inserted central point
evaluations.result: One-percent-scale pairwise-distance perturbations yield widely different attainable plots, and a central poison point destroys a previously separated visualization.
evaluations.baseline: Unperturbed inputs and PCA projections of the same inputs.

evaluations.setting: Credit-card fraud subset with 5,050 points in 30 dimensions, including 50 fraudulent users
evaluations.metric: Geometric outlier number in input and two-dimensional output
evaluations.result: t-SNE mixes fraudulent points into the bulk while PCA keeps most separated; across examples t-SNE rarely displays output outlier number above 0.2.
evaluations.baseline: PCA on the same representative subset.

evaluations.setting: BBC news data with 2,225 RoBERTa embeddings in 1,024 dimensions
evaluations.metric: Silhouette score relative to five ground-truth topics
evaluations.result: Injecting 220 poison points, about ten percent of the original count, halves t-SNE silhouette, whereas 1,100 far outliers, about fifty percent, do not degrade the displayed cluster structure.
evaluations.baseline: The unmodified t-SNE embedding and PCA behavior under the same additions.

limitations: Author-stated: additive invariance and input/output affinity asymmetry can also be useful, for example by filtering high-dimensional noise, so the results do not imply that t-SNE is uniformly inferior.
Author-stated: extension to other force-based dimensionality-reduction techniques is supported only by preliminary UMAP experiments.

Reviewer-identified: statements about all stationary points do not by themselves give the probability that a finite-iteration optimizer reaches a misleading point under common initialization, early-exaggeration, and perplexity defaults.
Reviewer-identified: several adversarial constructions use n-1 input dimensions or deliberately selected points, and the real-data examples do not quantify prevalence under non-adversarial sampling.

Reviewer-identified: the empirical comparisons emphasize PCA but do not compare diagnostic overlays, stability ensembles, or newer embedding-quality auditing methods that could warn users about distortion.
failure_modes: A user can interpret a crisp t-SNE cluster gap as evidence of strong input separation even when an arbitrarily weakly separated impostor has the same loss landscape.
Concentration of measure can put a data set near a simplex, where small distance changes or one central nearest-neighbor hub have disproportionate influence.
Outliers can be absorbed into an apparent cluster because the normalized output affinity cannot express their input-space extremity at stationarity.

Theorems about stationary embeddings may overpredict practical failures if typical optimization systematically selects a benign subset of stationary points; the paper does not estimate that selection effect.
reusable_insights: A visualization audit should test identifiability: search for materially different inputs that preserve the algorithm's sufficient statistic or objective landscape.
Mechanism-guided adversarial points can be a more revealing diagnostic than generic input noise.
Embedding claims should report input-space metrics and multiple projection baselines rather than treating visual gaps as measurements.
Distinguish impossibility of inference from frequency of failure: the first can be theorem-backed while the second needs a sampling protocol.
open_questions: Under standard early-exaggeration and initialization distributions, how often do the constructed ambiguous stationary regions attract optimization?
Can an efficiently computed certificate detect when an observed t-SNE plot has a low-salience impostor or is near a poison-point instability?
Which restrictions on intrinsic dimension, density, or sampling eliminate the additive-invariance counterexamples?
Can a visualization objective represent extreme outliers while retaining t-SNE's resistance to distance concentration?
How do the stationary-set non-identifiability results relate formally to the post-submission global-minimizer collapse results for nearly uniform spherical data?

competitive_landscape.title: Clustering with t-SNE, provably
competitive_landscape.difference: Linderman and Steinerberger prove contraction of well-separated clusters during early exaggeration under favorable separation and parameter scaling; this paper instead constructs inputs for which stationary outputs cannot identify separation strength.

competitive_landscape.title: An Analysis of the t-SNE Algorithm for Data Visualization
competitive_landscape.difference: Arora, Hu, and Kothari give recovery guarantees for suitably separated clusters and early-exaggeration dynamics; the reviewed work studies converse identifiability and failure constructions outside those guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: Theoretical Foundations of t-SNE for Visualizing High-Dimensional Clustered Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Cai and Ma characterize early exaggeration as graph-Laplacian power iteration and later amplification/stabilization phases; the reviewed paper proves ambiguity of stationary output geometry rather than convergence behavior under a clustered generative model.

competitive_landscape.title: T-SNE Is Not Optimized to Reveal Clusters in Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang, Chen, and Corander show false negatives and objective/visual-quality mismatch empirically on real data; this paper supplies explicit landscape identities, poison constructions, and an input-independent stationary outlier bound.

competitive_landscape.title: Compressibility Barriers to Neighborhood-Preserving Data Visualizations
competitive_landscape.difference: Snoeck, Bergam, and Verma prove dimension lower bounds for preserving graph neighborhoods in low-doubling and normed spaces, even with planted clusters; the reviewed paper is t-SNE-specific and identifies affinity mechanisms, cluster-salience ambiguity, poisoning, and outlier suppression.

competitive_landscape.title: Some Theoretical Limitations of t-SNE
competitive_landscape.difference: Li and Mossel study a later, overlapping negative-theory direction in which global minimizers collapse equidistant or high-dimensional spherical samples into a small ball. The reviewed paper instead establishes identical stationary sets across inputs of different cluster strength, small-perturbation non-identifiability, poison points, and a universal stationary outlier bound.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first systematic theoretical study of t-SNE false-positive and false-negative failure modes, including non-identifiability of cluster salience and extreme outliers.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Earlier theory mainly proves cluster recovery under separation assumptions, while earlier negative work is empirical or applies to generic low-dimensional neighborhood preservation. The paper derives exact t-SNE affinity and stationary-gradient results and backs them with mechanism-matched experiments.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest defensible novelty is the combination of stationary-set non-identifiability under additive distance shifts, a one-point cluster-masking construction, and an input-independent outlier-number bound. The later arXiv:2604.13295 independently develops theoretical t-SNE limitations for global minimizers of equidistant and spherical data, so a current account should present these as complementary negative theories rather than retain an unrestricted first-theory claim.

reviewer_notes: Read all 25 extracted PDF pages, including theorem statements, empirical appendices, and proofs at the level needed to check the claimed mechanisms. Page anchors refer to PDF pages. Primary arXiv records were searched by mechanism, evaluation/failure setting, and the paper's cited novelty language, then checked through 2026-08-23. The post-submission arXiv:2604.13295v1 PDF was also inspected beyond its abstract to distinguish its global-minimizer sphere-collapse results from this paper's stationary-set and outlier results. No code or theorem proof was independently rerun, so empirical prevalence and formal correctness remain author-reported where indicated.
